name: Multi-Table Investigations
goal: Connect tables without lying — find what doesn't match, and treat the gaps as findings, not nuisances.

brief.body: The PE firm's finance lead asked me a question I couldn't answer cleanly: 'Does total payments collected reconcile to total order revenue?' I said 'roughly.' Not good enough. Reconcile orders against payments to the rupee, explain every gap, and tell me if we're recognising any revenue we never actually collected. This ticket makes or breaks diligence.

clinic.title: Joins as investigation tools
clinic.body: INNER keeps matches and silently deletes everything else. LEFT keeps all left rows; unmatched ones surface as NULL on the right. The pattern LEFT JOIN … WHERE right.key IS NULL finds what's missing — orphan payments, unpaid orders, deprecated SKUs. In reconciliation, the unmatched rows are the entire point.

classwork.title: Build the cash reconciliation — together

steps.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS orphan_payments, ROUND(SUM(pmt.Amount),0) AS orphan_amount
FROM payments pmt
LEFT JOIN orders o ON pmt.OrderID = o.OrderID
WHERE o.OrderID IS NULL;
steps.checkpoint: 200 orphan payments totalling ~₹81.2 lakh — orders were purged. Flag to Ravi.

steps.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS unpaid_orders, ROUND(SUM(o.Revenue),0) AS uncollected_revenue
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN payments pmt ON o.OrderID = pmt.OrderID
WHERE pmt.OrderID IS NULL;
steps.checkpoint: 150 unpaid orders ~₹30.8 lakh recognised with no matching payment — the scary CFO number.

steps.instr: Classify matched-but-mismatched amounts — mind the branch order.
steps.sql:
SELECT
  CASE WHEN pmt.PaymentStatus='Refunded' THEN 'Refunded (cash returned)'
       WHEN pmt.Amount < o.Revenue THEN 'Underpaid / partial'
       WHEN pmt.Amount > o.Revenue THEN 'Overpaid / EMI rounding'
       ELSE 'Exact match' END AS gap_type,
  COUNT(*) AS orders,
  ROUND(SUM(pmt.Amount - o.Revenue), 0) AS net_gap_inr
FROM orders o JOIN payments pmt ON o.OrderID = pmt.OrderID
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY ABS(SUM(pmt.Amount - o.Revenue)) DESC;
steps.checkpoint: Check Refunded BEFORE the amount comparisons — otherwise refunds misclassify as 'underpaid'. The #1 reviewer trap this sprint.

classwork.reference:
SELECT 'orphan_payments' AS check_name, COUNT(*) AS records, ROUND(SUM(pmt.Amount),0) AS rupees
FROM payments pmt LEFT JOIN orders o ON pmt.OrderID=o.OrderID WHERE o.OrderID IS NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT 'unpaid_orders', COUNT(*), ROUND(SUM(o.Revenue),0)
FROM orders o LEFT JOIN payments pmt ON o.OrderID=pmt.OrderID WHERE pmt.OrderID IS NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT 'matched_amount_gap', COUNT(*), ROUND(SUM(pmt.Amount - o.Revenue),0)
FROM orders o JOIN payments pmt ON o.OrderID=pmt.OrderID;

tickets.title: Expose the revenue an INNER JOIN to products would hide
tickets.prompt: Prove how dangerous a reflexive INNER JOIN to products is. In ONE query (LEFT JOIN orders to products), return exactly these five columns in order: total_orders, total_revenue (rounded 0), orders_on_deprecated_skus, revenue_hidden_by_inner_join (rounded 0), pct_revenue_at_risk (rounded 2).
acceptanceCriteria: Single row, five columns in the stated order
Deprecated = ProductID absent from products (IS NULL after LEFT JOIN)
hints: LEFT JOIN products pr ON o.ProductID=pr.ProductID.
Deprecated rows are where pr.ProductID IS NULL.
Use SUM(CASE WHEN pr.ProductID IS NULL THEN … END) for the hidden counts/revenue.

tickets.title: Payment-method mix & digital penetration over time
tickets.prompt: Is COD declining as a share of orders? Join orders to payments and return, per year, exactly these four columns in order: OrderYear, cod_pct, digital_pct (everything except COD), upi_pct. Round every percentage to 1 decimal. One row per year, chronological.
hints: CTE joining orders to payments to get (OrderYear, PaymentMethod).
cod_pct = SUM(CASE WHEN PaymentMethod='COD' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)*100.0/COUNT(*).

tickets.title: Sale-event lift via a non-equi join
tickets.prompt: Did sale events actually lift revenue? Join orders to events where the order date falls between an event's start and end — a non-equi join most juniors have never written — and compare average daily revenue inside vs outside event windows.
acceptanceCriteria: Orders tagged in/out of an event window via BETWEEN on dates
Average daily revenue compared event vs non-event
hints: LEFT JOIN events e ON o.OrderDate BETWEEN e.StartDate AND e.EndDate.
Aggregate to daily revenue per window_type, then AVG.
An order in overlapping events multiplies — use EXISTS or SELECT DISTINCT to avoid double-count.
tickets.solution:
WITH tagged AS (
  SELECT o.OrderDate, o.Revenue,
    CASE WHEN e.EventID IS NOT NULL THEN 'Event' ELSE 'Non-event' END AS window_type
  FROM orders o
  LEFT JOIN events e ON o.OrderDate BETWEEN e.StartDate AND e.EndDate
),
daily AS (
  SELECT window_type, OrderDate, SUM(Revenue) AS day_rev FROM tagged GROUP BY window_type, OrderDate
)
SELECT window_type, COUNT(*) AS days, ROUND(AVG(day_rev),0) AS avg_daily_revenue
FROM daily GROUP BY window_type;
tickets.modelNote: Lift = (event avg / non-event avg - 1) * 100, computed from the two rows. Watch the overlapping-events edge case — it inflates an order's row via the LEFT JOIN.
